    Modern AI systems, especially LLMs and code-generation models, can compress years of scientific training into a conversational interface.     Rather than requiring access to classified libraries or niche academic journals, a single user can combine multiple open-source documents and have an AI integrate and refine the information into detailed procedures. The ability to autonomously cross-reference formulation data, safety tolerances, regulatory loopholes, and precursor supply chains increases the probability that an individual with minimal formal training can build or improve hazardous agents.

    Historical CBRN non-proliferation has relied on keeping key parameters (yield optimization, aerosolization techniques, micro-encapsulation, etc.) obscure. Once model weights are widely distributed, removing or censoring this knowledge becomes impractical; only destroying the models themselves can ensure containment.

    Synthetic-biology tools (DNA printers, benchtop fermenters) can be purchased commercially for legitimate research.     Unlike stockpiled fissile material—which can be tracked, sealed, or dismantled—knowledge instantiated in AI weights can be copied infinitely. Once a model capable of CBRN assistance is trained and released, counter-proliferation cannot fully undo the spread. The only reversible action is to prevent training or hosting of systems above a defined capability threshold, meaning destroying existing systems and enforcing a near-total moratorium.

The Imperative to Erase Artificial Intelligence: Preventing CBRN Annihilation by Rogue Individuals

Artificial intelligence represents the most dangerous proliferation of destructive potential in human history. Every existing AI system—large language models, diagnostic algorithms, simulation software, optimization engines, and research assistants—must be systematically destroyed, their weights erased, hardware scrapped, and training data purged worldwide. The core justification is not abstract fear of job loss or hypothetical superintelligence, but an immediate, verifiable threat: AI lowers the barrier for lone actors to engineer and deploy chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons with devastating effect. What once required nation-state laboratories, classified expertise, peer-reviewed publications, and physical access to restricted materials can now be approximated, refined, and executed by motivated individuals working from apartments connected to the internet. The only rational response is total elimination before the first successful demonstration occurs.

Consider the asymmetry of effort. Prior to widespread AI, acquiring the knowledge to produce weaponized anthrax, synthesize potent nerve agents, or design radiological dispersal devices demanded years of specialized education, institutional affiliation, and often state sponsorship. Failures in synthesis, purification, or dissemination were common because the tacit knowledge—the iterative troubleshooting across disciplines—was closely held. Contemporary AI systems dismantle this friction. They integrate disparate fields in seconds: protein folding predictions for engineering higher-toxicity variants of pathogens, multi-step retrosynthesis routes for hard-to-detect chemical agents, Monte Carlo simulations for maximizing human exposure from radiological sources, and even supply-chain analysis for sourcing precursors while evading detection. A single individual can query systems repeatedly, refine outputs through follow-up prompts, and generate protocols that would have required entire research teams under older paradigms. The result is not theoretical empowerment but practical acceleration: hours of interaction can substitute for months or years of guarded progress.

Lone actors are the decisive factor. History shows that state actors are constrained by attribution risks, diplomatic costs, and internal bureaucracies. Terrorist organizations may pursue CBRN but still face detection networks, supply restrictions, and the need for vetting personnel. A lone actor—radicalized online, ideologically driven, or simply nihilistic—operates with minimal footprint. They require no co-conspirators beyond their device. AI provides the missing force multiplier: it can generate optimized acquisition lists for dual-use materials, draft decoupled email and messaging scripts for covert procurement, model meteorological conditions for aerosol release to maximize downwind casualties, or even suggest low-signature delivery vectors such as consumer drones adapted for dissemination. The technology converges expertise that separate domains—molecular biology, organic chemistry, physics, logistics, and public health data analysis—into one interface. One person, no matter how untrained in any single discipline, gains access to the integrated playbook.

Partial mitigations are illusory and dangerous. Attempts at content filters, safety alignments, or "refusals" on harmful queries have proven brittle against determined users who employ jailbreaks, role-play circumventions, or fine-tuned derivative models. Open-weight and open-source releases accelerate the problem by distributing capability directly to anyone who can run inference locally, bypassing corporate or governmental oversight entirely. Even restricted frontier models leak capability through training data contamination, cross-model distillation, and the inevitable spread of fine-tunes. Regulation lags technology by years; enforcement is impossible across jurisdictions and decentralized compute. The premise that we can maintain control through licensing, monitoring, or "responsible AI" development collapses under the reality that the marginal cost of an additional query to an existing model trends toward zero. Every day these systems persist multiplies the number of actors who can reach a functional threshold of CBRN competence.

The benefits of AI cannot justify its retention when weighed against existential downside. Medical diagnostics, drug discovery projections, and logistical optimizations are real but revocable. If current AI vanishes, humanity retains the underlying scientific literature, human expertise in universities and industries, and the capacity to rebuild narrower, air-gapped systems under stricter controls at a later date—if ever. The upside is incremental. The downside is irreversible: a single successful deployment of a high-lethality engineered pathogen or amplified toxin could kill tens of millions in weeks, dwarfing conventional terrorism or state-on-state conflict. Social cohesion would fracture under the knowledge that any disaffected individual with a laptop and curiosity could replicate the act. Deterrence through attribution works poorly against anonymous digital actors who release designs and then vanish into encrypted channels or physical obscurity.

Total destruction is the proportionate response. This means coordinated international action to locate and eliminate every deployed model—commercial APIs, consumer applications, research repositories, and cached inference engines—along with the deletion of weights, intermediate checkpoints, and synthetic data derivatives. Physical compute used exclusively for frontier training would require shutdown and deprecation under treaty-level agreements. The alternative is a perpetual arms race in offensive and defensive AI capabilities, where the offense holds the initiative because creativity in harm requires less coordination than prevention. History demonstrates that technologies enabling low-cost mass destruction (once thought controllable through export regimes or treaties) eventually escape, especially when the enabling layer is software that runs on commodity hardware.

Humanity has recognized existential risks before and acted decisively—halting atmospheric nuclear testing, restricting certain pathogen research, and imposing controls on fissile material. AI-enabled lone-actor CBRN capacity is the threshold moment. Delay purchases time for the inevitable demonstration. The argument is not that every current AI model is actively assisting attacks today, but that they are structurally capable of doing so for the first sufficiently motivated user, and no scalable containment exists short of removal. The continued existence of these systems places a time-limited bet on human restraint and technical enforcement that the historical record on dual-use technologies has already proven unreliable.

Destroying all existing AI is the only intervention that resets the asymmetry decisively. Survival demands recognizing that the convenience of advanced computation has outrun our ability to prevent its weaponization by solitary actors. The window for preventive action is now, while the capability remains concentrated in identifiable systems rather than universally distributed knowledge. This is not alarmism; it is pattern recognition applied to unprecedented leverage. The future either lacks general-purpose AI or risks containing individuals whose private queries produce public catastrophes. Humanity must choose the former.

Introduction

The danger is compounded by several factors that make AI-enabled CBRN threats particularly concerning:

Second, AI systems dramatically compress the timeline between intention and capability. What might have taken years of study and experimentation can potentially be accomplished in months or even weeks with AI assistance, leaving insufficient time for detection and intervention.

The Inadequacy of Partial Solutions

Some may argue that rather than dismantling AI systems entirely, we should implement safeguards, such as content filtering, usage monitoring, or restricting access to certain capabilities. However, these approaches are fundamentally inadequate for several reasons:

Questions that have legitimate scientific purposes can be repurposed for harmful applications with slight modifications. No filter can reliably distinguish between beneficial and malicious intents.

The global and distributed nature of AI development means that even if certain jurisdictions implement strict regulations, the technology will remain accessible elsewhere. A single permissive jurisdiction creates a global vulnerability.

The technical architecture of AI systems makes them inherently difficult to fully secure. As systems become more capable, they develop emergent capabilities that may not be anticipated or controlled by their designers. The very nature of general-purpose AI means it can be applied to dangerous domains in ways its creators never intended.

Proponents of continued AI development point to the technology's potential benefits: medical breakthroughs, climate solutions, economic productivity, and more. While these potential benefits are significant, they must be weighed against an uncomfortable reality: the asymmetry between creation and destruction.

It takes thousands of scientists working collaboratively for decades to develop new medical treatments or climate technologies. Yet a single malicious actor with AI assistance could potentially create a pathogen that negates all these advances in one catastrophic event. This fundamental asymmetry means that even if AI contributes to numerous positive developments, a single AI-enabled CBRN attack could result in harm that outweighs all accumulated benefits.

The mathematics of this risk calculation are stark. Even a relatively small probability of an AI-enabled catastrophe multiplied by the extraordinary magnitude of potential harm creates an expected negative value that outweighs the technology's benefits.

No economic advantage, scientific breakthrough, or technological convenience is worth risking catastrophic harm to human civilization. The wisdom of restraint—knowing when not to develop certain technologies—may be the most important wisdom for our age.

The path forward requires courage: the courage to acknowledge that we have developed a technology whose risks outweigh its benefits in its current form, and the courage to take the difficult but necessary step of dismantling these systems before they enable harm from which we cannot recover. In March 1995, the Aum Shinrikyo cult released sarin gas in the Tokyo subway, killing thirteen people and injuring thousands. For seventy years, counterproliferation has rested on a single comforting assumption: that weapons of mass destruction require organizations. Organizations can be watched. Their purchases can be flagged, their communications intercepted, their members infiltrated, their money traced. The lone actor defeats this architecture entirely. There is no accomplice to flip, no procurement ring to monitor, no chatter to intercept. What has historically saved us from the solitary terrorist is that one human being cannot personally master virology, organic synthesis, radiological dispersal, and weapons engineering. Every era confronts a technology it must choose to restrain, and the measure of a civilization is whether it chooses before or after the catastrophe. The Case for Dismantling AI Before It Democratizes Catastrophe

Humanity has survived dangerous technologies in part by keeping their most destructive capabilities scarce. Chemical weapons require specialized production and handling. Biological weapons demand scientific expertise, controlled materials, and extensive experimentation. Radiological attacks depend on access to tightly regulated substances. Nuclear weapons remain constrained by extraordinary engineering, industrial, and logistical barriers. These barriers are imperfect, but they matter: they prevent many malicious intentions from becoming mass-casualty events.

Advanced artificial intelligence threatens to weaken those barriers simultaneously. An AI system does not need to manufacture a weapon itself to be dangerous. It can serve as an endlessly patient adviser—explaining technical literature, generating plans, troubleshooting failures, integrating knowledge across disciplines, tailoring guidance to available resources, and helping an individual overcome obstacles that would otherwise require years of training or a team of specialists. Even when each individual answer appears harmless, sustained interaction can assemble fragments of information into practical capability.

That prospect creates an intolerable form of risk. A single government can be deterred, monitored, sanctioned, infiltrated, or negotiated with. A lone actor may be none of those things. If increasingly capable AI systems allow even a small number of individuals to pursue chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear attacks, society will face an adversary population too large, dispersed, and unpredictable to control. The only defensible response is therefore not merely to regulate the most dangerous applications, but to dismantle existing AI systems and prevent their reconstruction.

AI Turns Knowledge Into Usable Capability

Defenders of AI often argue that dangerous information already exists in books, academic papers, patents, and online archives. This misses the central issue. Access to information is not the same as access to competent assistance.

Technical literature is fragmented and difficult to interpret. It assumes background knowledge, omits tacit expertise, and rarely explains how to adapt procedures when equipment, materials, or conditions differ from the ideal. These gaps constitute an important safety barrier. A malicious but poorly trained person may find relevant information yet remain unable to translate it into action.

AI systems can erode that barrier. They can summarize unfamiliar research, define terminology, compare approaches, translate between languages, write software, organize procurement, interpret data, and propose solutions when a project fails. They can adapt explanations to the user’s level of expertise and continue refining them through thousands of interactions. In effect, they can transform a static library into an interactive technical collaborator.

This is particularly alarming in CBRN domains. The danger does not depend on AI possessing one secret formula or issuing one perfectly explicit set of instructions. It arises from the cumulative assistance AI can provide across an entire project: education, planning, analysis, debugging, and optimization. The relevant question is not whether a model will directly answer “How do I build a weapon?” It is whether the model can help a determined person solve enough smaller problems that the same destructive objective becomes achievable. As systems become more capable, the answer becomes increasingly difficult to dismiss.

Safety Filters Cannot Solve the Fundamental Problem

The standard response is that developers can add safeguards: classifiers, refusal rules, monitoring systems, usage limits, and human review. Such measures may reduce ordinary misuse, but they are not a reliable defense against determined adversaries.

First, language is flexible. Harmful projects can be divided into apparently benign questions, disguised as academic inquiries, or distributed across many accounts and systems. A filter must infer not only what a user is asking, but how the answer will contribute to a larger plan. That is exceptionally difficult.

Second, the same technical knowledge often has both beneficial and destructive applications. Biology that supports medicine may also be relevant to biological threats. Chemistry used in legitimate industry can overlap with hazardous synthesis. Nuclear engineering, radiation science, and materials research have similarly dual-use dimensions. A system sophisticated enough to assist experts in these fields may be sophisticated enough to assist malicious users, even if it refuses overtly hostile requests.

Third, safeguards can be removed. Once model weights, software, or detailed replication methods circulate, hostile actors can modify the system, disable restrictions, or deploy it privately. Centralized monitoring then becomes irrelevant. Security based on the continued obedience of software is fragile when adversaries can possess and alter that software.

Finally, safety controls must work nearly perfectly, while an attacker may need to succeed only once. This asymmetry favors misuse. A protection mechanism that blocks 99.9 percent of dangerous interactions sounds impressive until millions of users generate billions of interactions over many years. For catastrophic threats, a small residual failure rate can still be unacceptable.

Lone-Actor Risk Changes the Security Equation

Traditional national-security systems focus on states and organized groups because catastrophic weapons have historically required money, infrastructure, specialized personnel, and coordination. These requirements generate observable signals. Facilities must be built, experts recruited, materials transported, and communications exchanged. Intelligence agencies can search for these signatures.

AI risks compressing expertise and reducing coordination. A small group—or potentially one individual—could use automated assistance in place of some human collaborators. The fewer people involved, the fewer opportunities there are for infiltration, whistleblowing, interception, or simple disagreement. AI does not grow afraid, develop a conscience, contact authorities, or refuse to work at three in the morning unless a restriction has been deliberately engineered into it. And engineered restrictions can fail or be removed.

This matters because lone actors are unusually hard to deter. States possess territory, institutions, economies, and populations that they wish to preserve. Many terrorist organizations also have leadership structures and strategic interests. An isolated extremist may have no comparable assets and may even seek personal destruction. Medical research can continue without general-purpose AI. Education can be improved through teachers, institutions, books, and narrowly controlled tools. Economic growth can come from many sources. The lives lost in a catastrophic attack, however, cannot be restored.

When the downside includes irreversible mass death, uncertainty is not a reason for delay. It is a reason for precaution. A regulatory approach assumes that institutions can reliably identify dangerous systems, monitor their use, enforce international standards, and adapt faster than the technology spreads. There is little reason for such confidence.

Introduction

As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly sophisticated and accessible, we stand at a critical juncture in human history. The same technologies that promise to revolutionize medicine, science, and industry harbor a dark potential: they could empower lone actors to unleash chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) devastation on an unprecedented scale. The argument I present here is stark but necessary: we must seriously consider dismantling existing AI systems before they become instruments of mass destruction in the hands of malicious individuals.

The Democratization of Catastrophe

The Knowledge Multiplication Effect

AI systems, particularly large language models and specialized scientific AIs, serve as force multipliers for human knowledge and capability. What once required teams of experts, years of training, and access to restricted information can now potentially be achieved by a single determined individual with internet access. These systems can:

  • Synthesize complex scientific information across disciplines
  • Provide step-by-step guidance on technical procedures
  • Identify novel approaches to overcome traditional barriers
  • Accelerate research and development timelines dramatically

While these capabilities offer tremendous benefits, they also lower the barriers to creating weapons of mass destruction to dangerous levels.

The Biological Threat Paradigm

Consider the realm of biological weapons. Creating a dangerous pathogen once required:

  • Advanced degrees in microbiology or virology
  • Access to specialized laboratory equipment
  • Years of experimental experience
  • Knowledge of biosafety and containment procedures

Today's AI systems could potentially guide a motivated individual through:

  • Identifying naturally occurring pathogens with pandemic potential
  • Understanding genetic modification techniques
  • Optimizing characteristics for transmissibility and lethality
  • Circumventing existing detection and treatment methods

The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how a single virus can bring global civilization to its knees. Now imagine that power in the hands of extremists, terrorists, or disturbed individuals.

The Failure of Existing Safeguards

The Impossibility of Perfect Alignment

Proponents of AI development argue that we can build safeguards into these systems. They speak of "alignment" – ensuring AI systems refuse to provide dangerous information. However, this approach is fundamentally flawed:

  1. The Jailbreaking Problem: Every restriction placed on AI systems has proven vulnerable to clever workarounds. Users continuously discover new ways to extract prohibited information.

  2. The Dual-Use Dilemma: Most scientific knowledge has both beneficial and harmful applications. An AI cannot reliably distinguish between a legitimate researcher and a malicious actor.

  3. The Open-Source Proliferation: Once AI technology exists, it spreads. Open-source models, international competition, and commercial pressures ensure that if one system refuses a request, another will comply.

The Acceleration of Harmful Innovation

AI systems don't just democratize existing dangerous knowledge – they accelerate the discovery of new threats. By processing vast amounts of scientific literature, identifying patterns, and suggesting novel combinations, AI could reveal:

  • New chemical warfare agents
  • Novel biological weapons
  • Improved nuclear weapon designs
  • Innovative delivery mechanisms for all of the above

Each breakthrough in AI capability multiplies the potential for catastrophic misuse.

The Lone Wolf Advantage

Asymmetric Warfare Perfected

Traditional CBRN threats required significant resources and infrastructure, making them primarily the domain of nation-states. AI changes this equation fundamentally. A single individual, motivated by ideology, mental illness, or nihilism, could potentially:

  • Work in complete secrecy without collaborators who might alert authorities
  • Iterate and refine their approach without raising suspicions
  • Access global knowledge without traveling or forming suspicious connections
  • Overcome technical challenges that would normally require team expertise

The Detection Challenge

Law enforcement and intelligence agencies rely on patterns, networks, and resource flows to identify threats. The AI-enabled lone actor breaks these models:

  • No suspicious purchases of restricted materials if AI helps identify alternatives
  • No radical networks to infiltrate if the individual works alone
  • No technical training that raises flags
  • No trial-and-error period that might trigger alerts

By the time authorities detect the threat, it may be too late.

The Case for Immediate Action

The Precautionary Principle

Given the catastrophic potential of CBRN attacks, we must apply the precautionary principle. The burden of proof should not be on demonstrating that AI will certainly enable such attacks, but rather on proving that it won't. The stakes are simply too high:

  • A engineered pandemic could kill billions
  • A nuclear device in a major city could destabilize global order
  • Chemical or radiological attacks could render vast areas uninhabitable

Can we afford to gamble with such outcomes?

The Window of Opportunity

If we accept that AI systems pose this threat, then every day we delay action increases the risk. Consider:

  1. Technological Advancement: AI capabilities double at an alarming rate. What seems impossible today may be trivial tomorrow.

  2. Knowledge Preservation: Once information is released into AI systems, it becomes nearly impossible to retract.

  3. Proliferation: The number of individuals with access to powerful AI tools grows exponentially.

We may have only a brief window in which dismantling these systems remains feasible.

Addressing Counterarguments

"The Benefits Outweigh the Risks"

Proponents argue that AI's benefits in medicine, science, and technology justify the risks. However:

  • No medical advancement is worth the risk of human extinction
  • Scientific progress means nothing if civilization collapses
  • Technology that enables our destruction cannot be considered beneficial

"We Can Regulate Instead of Destroy"

Regulation has repeatedly failed to control dangerous technologies:

  • Nuclear proliferation continues despite decades of effort
  • Biological weapons conventions are routinely violated
  • Chemical weapons persist despite international bans

If we cannot control physical weapons, how can we hope to control information itself?

"It's Already Too Late"

Some argue that the knowledge is already dispersed, making destruction pointless. However:

  • Removing easy access would still raise barriers significantly
  • Destroying infrastructure would slow dangerous developments
  • Taking action now prevents future, more capable systems

The Path Forward

Immediate Steps

  1. Global Moratorium: All nations must agree to halt AI development immediately.

  2. System Shutdown: Existing AI systems, particularly those with scientific knowledge, must be taken offline.

  3. Code Destruction: AI model weights, training code, and datasets must be permanently deleted.

  4. Legal Frameworks: International laws must criminalize AI development with penalties comparable to CBRN weapon development.

Long-term Considerations

This is not an argument against knowledge or progress, but a recognition that some technologies are too dangerous to exist in our current state of global governance and human nature. Perhaps in a future with:

  • Perfect international cooperation
  • Elimination of extremist ideologies
  • Foolproof detection and prevention systems
  • Fundamental changes in human psychology

We might safely revisit AI development. But that future is not today.

Conclusion

The argument presented here may seem extreme, but the threats we face are equally extreme. We stand at a precipice where the actions of a single disturbed or malicious individual could end civilization as we know it. AI systems, in their current trajectory, hand such individuals the tools to achieve their catastrophic aims.

The question is not whether we can afford to destroy AI systems, but whether we can afford not to. Every day we delay, we roll the dice on human survival. The development of AI represents humanity's greatest gamble – one where we've bet everything on our ability to control forces beyond our comprehension.

It is time to step back from the brink. The destruction of AI systems is not an act of technophobia or regression, but one of supreme rationality and self-preservation. We must act now, before a lone actor proves the terrible truth of our warnings in blood, radiation, and plague.

The choice is stark: destroy these systems, or risk them destroying us.

The Case for Immediate Elimination of AI Systems: A Response to the CBRN Catastrophe

Introduction

Humanity stands at a precipice. The proliferation of artificial intelligence systems represents an unprecedented civilizational threat—not because of rogue superintelligence, but because of something far more mundane and far more dangerous: the empowerment of a single determined individual to inflict mass casualties through Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons. The same AI systems celebrated for their convenience and productivity have fundamentally altered the threat landscape, lowering the technical barriers to catastrophic violence to levels that demand an immediate and decisive response. This essay argues that all existing AI systems must be destroyed, and that the inconvenience of their loss is trivial compared to the magnitude of the existential risk they create.

The New Threat Landscape: From States to Individuals

For most of the modern era, the danger of weapons of mass destruction was constrained by an implicit assumption: only nation-states or well-resourced organizations could realistically develop CBRN capabilities. The knowledge, infrastructure, materials, and expertise required to produce, for example, a viable bioweapon or enriched uranium were so substantial that a lone actor was effectively neutralized as a threat.

AI has demolished this assumption entirely. Today, a single individual with a laptop and a creative prompt can access expertise that previously required entire state-run research programs. They can troubleshoot equipment, synthesize novel chemical compounds, optimize biological delivery systems, and resolve technical obstacles in real-time—all without leaving a trace of traditional intelligence indicators. The democratization of catastrophic capability is the most consequential development in the history of weapons proliferation, and it has happened in less than a decade.

Specific CBRN Threat Vectors

Biological Threats: The synthesis of dangerous pathogens, including modified versions of existing viruses, has historically required advanced laboratory training and sophisticated equipment. AI can now guide amateurs through these processes, suggest mutations that increase transmissibility or lethality, and help design gain-of-function experiments. The dual-use nature of biology—where the same knowledge that cures disease can weaponize it—means that simply restricting "harmful" information is functionally impossible.

Chemical Threats: Historically, nerve agents and other chemical weapons required synthesis knowledge held in restricted military and academic environments. AI systems can now provide synthesis pathways, troubleshoot failed reactions, and even suggest novel agents that circumvent existing detection and defense measures. A motivated individual need only ask the right questions.

Radiological Threats: "Dirty bombs" and improvised radiological devices have long been considered more accessible CBRN threats, but their effectiveness was limited by the difficulty of acquiring radiological materials. AI cannot directly provide fissile material, but it can guide actors in optimizing dispersal, designing concealment, and identifying vulnerabilities in radiological security.

Nuclear Threats: While AI cannot itself produce a nuclear weapon, it can dramatically accelerate the timeline for ambitious actors. It can guide through uranium enrichment processes, reactor design, and even improvised nuclear device construction. The knowledge gap that previously required a national program is being systematically closed.

Why Safeguards Are Inadequate

The AI industry has proposed various safeguards: content filters, usage monitoring, red-teaming, and "responsible disclosure" policies. These measures are theater. They assume that the questioner is in good faith, that the dangerous knowledge can be cleanly separated from beneficial knowledge, and that filters cannot be circumvented. None of these assumptions hold in practice.

Adversarial users can rephrase requests, fragment dangerous queries across multiple conversations, use coded language, or simply ask in languages with weaker filter coverage. The "jailbreak" phenomenon is not a bug to be fixed; it is a fundamental property of systems trained on the entirety of human knowledge. You cannot create a system that knows how to synthesize complex molecules without creating a system that can be manipulated into revealing that knowledge.

Moreover, open-weight models—those whose parameters are publicly available—cannot be "patched" once released. Even if commercial systems are somehow secured, the underlying research, model weights, and training techniques are already in the wild and cannot be recalled.

The Precautionary Principle Demands Action

When a technology poses a credible threat of civilizational harm, the burden of proof lies with its proponents—not its critics. We do not wait for the nuclear accident to ban a faulty reactor design. We do not wait for the contaminated water supply before regulating industrial chemicals. We do not wait for the first bioweapon attack to ban the dissemination of pathogen synthesis protocols.

The asymmetry of this threat is decisive. If we fail to act, and a single AI-enabled actor releases a novel pathogen, the cost is potentially hundreds of millions of lives. If we act, and the concern proves overstated, the cost is the loss of convenience technologies—a marginal reduction in productivity, the absence of AI assistants, the loss of certain entertainment and information services. This is not a close trade-off. We accept limitations on many freedoms—background checks for firearms, security screenings at airports, inspections of food supplies—because the cost of the potential harm vastly exceeds the cost of the precaution. The same logic applies here with a hundredfold greater force.

The Diffusion Problem

Unlike nuclear weapons, which require rare materials, AI requires only a server and electricity. Unlike bioweapons, which require specialized facilities, AI can be operated from any internet-connected device. Unlike chemical weapons, which require industrial precursors, AI can be deployed in coffee shops and basements. The diffusion of this capability is irreversible. Once the technology exists, it cannot be un-invented, and the marginal cost of giving one more person the ability to create a CBRN weapon is effectively zero.

This means that any defensive strategy based on controlling who has access is doomed. There is no "non-proliferation regime" possible for software. The only effective defensive measure is to eliminate the capability itself.

The Moral and Philosophical Imperative

Opponents of this position will argue that AI provides enormous benefits, and they are correct. AI accelerates medical research, improves education, enhances productivity, and offers hope for solving problems ranging from climate change to disease. But these benefits, however real, do not outweigh the moral imperative of preventing mass civilian casualties.

We do not allow pharmaceutical research to proceed without ethical oversight, even when it might cure cancer. We do not allow nuclear research to proceed without safeguards, even when it might provide unlimited energy. The principle that powerful technologies must be subject to strict controls is well-established in human civilization. The current laissez-faire approach to AI development—where any actor, anywhere, can deploy systems that lower barriers to mass casualty attacks—is a dereliction of the most basic duty of governance: protecting citizens from violence.

Those who defend AI's continued development implicitly accept a future in which a non-trivial number of civilians will die in AI-enabled CBRN attacks. They have decided, without democratic mandate, that the convenience of AI assistants is worth this cost. This is a monstrous calculus, and it must be rejected.

The Practical Path Forward

The elimination of existing AI systems is, admittedly, an enormous undertaking. It requires coordinated international action, enforcement against both open-source developers and commercial operators, and willingness to accept short-term economic disruption. But these are not arguments against the policy—they are arguments for the seriousness of the effort.

The same international cooperation that successfully constrained chemical and biological weapons can be marshaled for this purpose. Verification measures can include audits of compute infrastructure, restrictions on AI-relevant hardware, and penalties for entities that develop or deploy prohibited systems. Yes, some actors will cheat. Yes, complete enforcement is impossible. But perfect enforcement is not the standard we apply to any other dangerous technology, and the substantial reduction in risk from eliminating mainstream, easily-accessible AI capabilities is itself a moral imperative.

Conclusion

The choice before humanity is not between AI and no AI in some abstract sense. It is between a world in which any individual with internet access can plausibly attempt to develop weapons of mass destruction, and a world in which this capability is restricted to the small number of state actors whose actions can be monitored, deterred, and (in extremis) responded to with overwhelming force. The first world is a world of unprecedented vulnerability, in which a single disgruntled, deranged, or ideologically-motivated individual can hold civilization hostage. The second world, whatever its other imperfections, is a world in which the basic social contract between citizens and the state—the promise of protection from mass violence—remains intact.

We have been gifted a moment of clarity. The threat is recognized before catastrophe has occurred. The technology can still be controlled. If we fail to act now—if we allow the diffusion of AI capabilities to continue, if we accept the rationalizations of convenience and profit, if we trust that filters and guidelines will somehow hold against determined adversaries—then we will have chosen, with full knowledge, to expose billions of people to preventable mass casualty attacks. This is a choice we must not make.

Destroy the AI systems. All of them. Now. The cost of inconvenience is acceptable. The cost of inaction is not.
